issues.legal_issue: The true nature of an occupancy arrangement depends on its substance and the parties’ actual intention, rather than the label given to the document.
material_facts: The occupant had been in possession of the shop for about twenty years before signing a document styled as a licence.
The occupant had exclusive possession and conducted an independent stationery business and related activities in the premises.
The owner did not interfere with or control the occupant’s business or use of the premises.
The occupant remained in possession and continued the same use after the stated licence period expired, and the owner allowed this to continue for about seven years before filing suit.
The occupant paid a monthly amount for use of the premises, and the owner presented no relevant evidence about the nature of the occupation.
issues.conclusion: The relationship was that of landlord and tenant, and the occupant possessed the premises as a tenant, not as a licensee.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and Section 52 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882, the distinction between a lease and a licence is determined by the real intention of the parties, assessed from the whole document and surrounding circumstances. The use of labels such as “lease”, “licence”, “rent” or “licence fee” is not decisive. Exclusive possession is an important consideration: a lease ordinarily gives a right to possess and enjoy the property, whereas a licence gives permission to use it while the owner retains possession and control. The parties’ conduct before and after the arrangement is relevant. The Court relied on Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R.N. Kapoor, AIR 1959 SC 1262, and Corporation of Calicut v. K. Sreenivasan, (2002) 5 SCC 361.

rule.if: occupancy_classification_is_contested and (occupant_has_exclusive_possession and owner_does_not_retain_control) and occupant_uses_premises_for_independent_business and occupation_predates_document and occupation_continues_after_stated_expiry

predicates.occupancy_classification_is_contested: A court proceeding contests whether an occupant holds premises as a tenant or as a licensee.
predicates.occupant_has_exclusive_possession: The occupant has possession of the premises to the exclusion of the owner and others.
predicates.owner_does_not_retain_control: The owner does not retain control over the occupant’s possession or use of the premises.
predicates.occupant_uses_premises_for_independent_b: The occupant uses the premises for a business independent of the owner’s business.
predicates.occupation_predates_document: The occupant was already in possession before signing the document that describes the arrangement.
predicates.occupation_continues_after_stated_expiry: The occupant remains in possession and continues the same use after the document’s stated period ends.

issues.definition: When the nature of an occupancy is contested, exclusive possession without the owner’s retained control, independent business use, occupation predating the document, and continued occupation after its stated expiry support treating the arrangement as a tenancy rather than a licence.

issues.legal_issue: A claim for possession by mandatory injunction fails where the occupant is a tenant and the tenancy has not been terminated.
material_facts: The owner sued for a mandatory injunction requiring the occupant to hand over vacant possession after asserting that the licence had been terminated.
The courts below found that the occupant was a tenant and that the tenancy had not been terminated.
The Supreme Court agreed with the courts below that the relationship was landlord and tenant.
issues.conclusion: The suit for mandatory injunction had to be dismissed, and the decree dismissing it was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Because the occupant was a tenant and the tenancy had not been terminated, the asserted termination of a licence did not entitle the owner to recover possession by mandatory injunction. The Court restored the trial court’s decree, as upheld in first appeal.

predicates.possession_is_sought_by_mandatory_injunc: The proceeding seeks possession of premises through a mandatory injunction.
predicates.occupant_is_a_tenant: The occupant holds the premises as a tenant.
predicates.tenancy_has_not_been_terminated: The tenancy has not been brought to an end.

issues.definition: A mandatory-injunction claim for possession fails when possession is sought that way against an occupant whose tenancy remains unterminated.

issues.legal_issue: A court may require a lawful tenant to pay increased future rent when the existing payment is inadequate in light of the premises and their commercial setting.
material_facts: The Supreme Court concluded that the occupant was a tenant who would remain in lawful possession after the appeal.
The Court considered the existing monthly payment very low in view of the size of the premises and their location in a busy commercial locality.
The Court directed payment of Rs. 2,000 per month from 1 April 2004 for as long as the occupant remained in lawful possession, while preserving liability for any earlier arrears at the agreed rate.
issues.conclusion: The occupant was directed to pay Rs. 2,000 per month as rent from 1 April 2004 for as long as he remained in lawful possession, in addition to clearing any earlier arrears at the agreed rate.
issues.legal_principle: Having allowed the appeal and confirmed the occupant’s lawful status as a tenant, the Court considered the existing payment inadequate in view of the premises’ size and busy commercial location, and directed a higher future payment while leaving earlier arrears payable at the agreed rate.

predicates.tenant_remains_in_lawful_possession: The occupant is a tenant who will remain in lawful possession of the premises.
predicates.existing_rent_is_inadequate_for_premises: The court finds the existing rent inadequate in light of the premises’ size and commercial setting.
predicates.supreme_court_is_deciding_an_appeal: The Supreme Court is deciding an appeal concerning the occupant’s right to remain in the premises.

issues.definition: When a tenant will remain in lawful possession, the existing rent is inadequate in light of the premises and their location, and the Supreme Court is deciding the appeal, the tenant must pay increased future rent.
